title: Language and Interior
premise: Edmund Thornbury, a woman who has spent thirty years writing postcards to her family's burned-down house, attends her mother's funeral where a stranger calls the family by their true, discarded surname. The stranger, a solicitor named Vera Okonkwo, reveals that Edmund's grandfather stole the name, the house, and a fortune from a business partner—and the rightful heirs want acknowledgment before the estate is sealed. As Edmund investigates, she realizes her lifelong silence was inherited too, a corruption passed down like the property itself. In the end, Edmund publicly renounces her claim to the Thornbury name at the reading of the will, speaks her grandfather's partner's name aloud at last, and mails one final postcard—not to the burned house, but to the living heirs, signed with her real name.
about_author: I. M. Dravenmoor is the pen name of a former archivist who spent a decade cataloging unclaimed letters in municipal storage, a job that taught her how much of a life fits on a postcard. Language and Interior is her second novel, following a widely praised debut about a translator who loses her mother tongue.

chapters.title: The Smile That Ends Conversations
chapters.summary: Edmund's POV. At her mother's funeral, Edmund performs flawless grief and deflects every condolence with her practiced smile, revealing her habit of postcards to the ruined house on Marsh Lane. When Vera Okonkwo approaches and calls the family by the name 'Ashcombe,' Edmund's armor cracks for the first time in years. Emotional beat: the terror of being seen after a lifetime of curated invisibility.

chapters.title: What the Deeds Don't Say
chapters.summary: Edmund's POV, with interleaved excerpts of her unsent letters. Vera presents documents showing Edmund's grandfather, Elias Ashcombe, took the Thornbury identity after his partner's death in suspicious circumstances. Edmund resists, defending the family myth, but the house's burned ruins and her mother's sealed correspondence begin to contradict her. Emotional beat: the vertigo of discovering one's inheritance is built on erasure.

chapters.title: The Reading of the Names
chapters.summary: Edmund's POV, climaxing at the will reading. The Thornbury relatives close ranks, offering Edmund money to dismiss Vera and keep the name clean; her cousin threatens to expose her postcard habit as madness. Cornered between complicity and exile, Edmund stands before the assembled family and speaks the name Ashcombe aloud for the first time, renouncing her share. Emotional beat: the costly, liberating rupture with belonging-as-silence.

chapters.title: Postscript, Marsh Lane
chapters.summary: Edmund's POV, weeks later. She visits the ashes of the old house with Vera, scatters her mother's unsent letters, and writes one final postcard to the surviving Ashcombe heirs, signing her true name. The smile she perfected is gone; in its place is an ordinary, unguarded face. Emotional beat: quiet resolution—grief finally spoken, inheritance transformed from property into acknowledgment.
